# Welcome to the official documentation of the Yggio API

The API consists of the following categories:

- **Authorization**
- **Apps**
- **Users**
- **Usergroups**
- **Data Listings**
- **DeviceGroups**
- **Organizations**
- **Iotnodes**
- **Connectors**
- **ClientApps**
- **Translators**
- **Locations**
- **LocationsV2**
- **Zones**
- **Channels**
- **BasicCredentialsSets**
- **ReservedMqttTopics**
- **Jobs**
- **Logos**
- **Logs**
- **AccessRights**
- **Reports**
- **Dashboards**
- **Geofences**
- **Images**
- **Roles**
- **Rules**
- **Calculations**
- **AlmanacFleetJobs**
- **AlmanacAutoUpdate**
- **VsmApps**
- **AppUpgradeJobs**

## 🔒 Authentication

Every call requires you to be authenticated, except for the following:

1. `POST /auth/local`
2. `POST /users`

To authenticate yourself, do the following:

1. Use the `POST /auth/local` endpoint. Include your username and password in the body.
2. Save the **token value** you get in response.
3. For all future API calls, use the token value in a **HTTP request header** as follows: "Bearer: [token value]". For Swagger you press the **Authorize button** and insert the token value.

## 🚦 Status codes

All requests will be responded with one out of the following status codes:

- `200` Success
- `201` Success - resource created
- `202` Success - request accepted for processing
- `204` Success - resource deleted
- `400` Bad request
- `401` Unauthorized
- `404` Not found
- `409` Conflict
- `500` Internal server error

If you have any questions or if you have found an error, please feel free to contact us.

get.description:
Returns all iotnodes that matches the query filter and are currently accessible by the user.

Response body can have additional attributes depending on which type it is.

You can query on any and multiple fields, for example:

`?connector=5fc86d62078fb9bbe0773ebd&name=strips101,strips102`

Name and devEui are provided below as examples, but you can query on any field.

### Pagination

A maximum of 2000 iotnodes can be fetched on one request. Pagination is done with the cursor pagination method.

To use pagination, `cursorId`, `cursorDirection` and `orderBy` needs to be supplied.

Full pagination is only supported for `_id`, `name` and `reportedAt`.

To use pagination with other properties, you need to also filter on the property you are ordering by.

To get the next page you need to include `orderBy`, `cursorDirection=next` and set `cursorId` to the orderBy property of the last iotnode in the previous response.

Example: `orderBy=name` `cursorDirection=next` `cursorId=NameOfLastDevice`

To get the previous page you need to include `orderBy`, `cursorDirection=prev` and set `cursorId` to the orderBy property of the first iotnode in the previous response.

Example: `orderBy=name` `cursorDirection=prev` `cursorId=NameOfFirstDevice`

get.description:
Returns data listings.

Each listing is returned without its `images` gallery; fetch it with
`GET /data-listings/{dataListingId}`. The `icon` is included.

Use the optional `filter` query parameter to narrow the result set. The value must be a
JSON-stringified object.

Supported filter keys:

- `name`
- `city` (case-insensitive substring; matches top-level `interventionCity` and per-dataset `dataSet.interventionCity`)
- `tags`
- `projects`
- `interventionTypes`
- `kpiCodes`
- `kpiTypes`
- `dataProcessorIds`
- `livingLabsAreaIds`
- `dataSetIds` (one id or an array; matches the per-dataset `dataSet.id` of Elaborator listings; GiC datasets use `gicDatasetIds`)
- `gicAreaIds`
- `gicLivingLabsActorIds`
- `gicStakeholderIds`
- `gicInterventionIds`
- `gicAssessmentToolIds`
- `gicDataProcessorIds`
- `gicDatasetIds`
- `gicKpiIds`
- `gicCoEvaluationMethodIds`
- `gicExAnteIds`
- `gicExPostIds`

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description:
JSON-stringified filter object.

Example: `filter={"projects":["elaborator"],"tags":["mobility"],"kpiTypes":["KeyPerformanceIndicatorGeneralMobilityExpansion"]}`

Create a new data listing.

Set `project` to choose the payload shape:

- `basic`
- `elaborator`

the created identifier rather than the full document, so fetch the listing afterwards if you
need the full resource.

put.description:

Needs the data listing update right of the caller's role. The image is stored as a
dataListingIcon bound to the listing, readable by every user while the listing shows it,
and managed only through the listing. Replaces and deletes the listing's previous uploaded
icon. The legacy icon field is left as it is.
The file must be image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and at most 8 MB.

Returns 404 when the listing does not exist, and 400 when no valid image is uploaded,
including one larger than 8 MB.

Uploads an image and appends it to the gallery of a data listing (imageIds).

Needs the data listing update right of the caller's role, the same as PUT /data-listings/{id}.

the listing shows it, and managed only through the listing: reorder or remove gallery images
by sending imageIds to PUT /data-listings/{id}. The legacy images field is left as it is.
The file must be image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and at most 8 MB. A gallery holds at most
100 images.

Returns 404 when the listing does not exist, 400 when no valid image is uploaded,
including one larger than 8 MB, and 422 when the gallery already holds 100 images.

Creates a location owned by the caller. Add zones to it with `POST /zones`.

Requires the admin role (the editor role may not create locations) and the
`locations_v2_active` account flag.

403.description:
The role may not create locations (plain text `Forbidden`), or `LMV2_NOT_ENABLED`: the
caller lacks the `locations_v2_active` account flag.

get.summary: List locations and zones as a tree
get.description:
Returns the locations the caller can see, each with its zones, and each zone with the
dashboards in it that the caller can read. Locations and zones are sorted by name, and a
zone's dashboards are in the zone's order. Not paginated.

A location or zone the caller cannot read is included only when it holds something the
caller can read, as a stub (`access: path`) that places it: a location around a readable
zone or dashboard, a zone around a readable dashboard.

Allowed for every role.

413.description: `LMV2_TOO_MANY_NODES`: the caller can see more than 2000 locations or 20000 zones (`limit`).

get.summary: Count open alarms per location, zone and dashboard
get.description:
Counts the devices on the caller's visible dashboards (see `GET /locations-v2/tree`) by
their worst open alarm: unacknowledged device logs with priority `severe` or `high`. A
zone counts the devices of its dashboards, and a location those of its zones, each device
once. Only dashboards the caller can read count, so a node reached by `access: path` counts
only what the caller can read inside it.

A device whose alarms the caller cannot see, because it cannot read the device, is counted
in `unmonitored` and nowhere else. A deleted device counts nowhere. Device ids are never
returned. Computed on every call and not paginated.

Requires a role that may read both locations and logs.

Start an over-the-air GNSS almanac push to a set of LoRa devices.

The almanac image is fetched from the semtech-lora-cloud connector, split into
data-rate sized chunks and sent as confirmed fPort 21 downlinks. Each device
acknowledges a chunk with a checksum uplink before the next one is sent, so a
push runs for minutes to hours depending on the data rate.

Returns immediately with the job ids; follow progress on
`GET /almanac-fleet-jobs/{almanacJobId}/detail`.

Devices whose data rate is below `minAcceptableDr` are recorded as `skipped` and
receive no downlinks. The caller must have write access to every requested device,
and no device may already have a push in flight.

delete.description:
Remove several almanac fleet pushes in one request, so a long list can be cleared
without one call per push.

Only the caller's own pushes are matched, so ids belonging to another user are
silently skipped rather than reported as missing: compare `deletedCount` with the
number of ids you sent if you need to know. As with the single delete, this removes
only the progress records - downlinks already queued on the LNS may still be
delivered.

Only the user who created the job can read it.

Cancel an almanac fleet push. Devices that have not been started yet are left

may still reach the devices, so a device may end up with a partial almanac.

Only the user who created the job can cancel it.

`/almanac-fleet-jobs/{almanacJobId}/detail`.

settings of each subscription and when it was last pushed to.

with more than that sees only the first page. A device's own subscription is also on the

put.description:
Subscribe a set of LoRa devices to automatic almanac updates, or cancel their
subscription.

A periodic sweep starts a real almanac push - the same transfer as
`POST /almanac-fleet-jobs` - for any subscribed device whose last push is older than
`intervalDays`. Each push runs with the authority of whoever created the subscription, so
subscribing is authorized exactly like starting a push by hand: write access to every
device, and write or admin access to every connector the frames would go through.

A manual push to a subscribed device also resets its interval, so an almanac refreshed by
hand does not get repeated by the sweep minutes later.

Enabling replaces any existing subscription outright rather than patching it, so send the
full set of settings you want.

Every device must be on a network server the almanac can be sent through - ChirpStack or
Netmore - or the request is a 422 naming the ones that are not. If a device later moves to
another network server, the sweep records the reason on its subscription and stops retrying
until the subscription is written again.

get.description:
Return the VSM applications the caller has access to.

The response carries the parsed metadata only, never the rule frames or the rule-memory
image - those exist for the upgrade driver and never leave the server. It also leaves out
`mapData`, which is tens of kB per app: read a single app for that. Use
`/vsm-apps/{vsmAppId}/file` to get the uploaded file back.

`name`, `fileHash` and `targetCrc32` filter on exact matches. `targetCrc32` is the useful
one operationally: it is the value a tracker reports on fPort 15, so it answers "which of
my apps is this device running".

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Filter on an exact display name.

parameters.name: fileHash
parameters.description: Filter on the sha256 of the uploaded bytes, lowercase hex.

parameters.name: targetCrc32
parameters.description:
Filter on the unsigned CRC32 of the fully loaded rule memory, as a decimal number - the
value a tracker reports on fPort 15.

post.description:
Upload a Sensative VSM application (`.vso`) so it can be programmed onto trackers.

The file is parsed on upload, not on push: the rule lines are laid out into the device's
2048-byte rule memory, the per-rule downlink frames are derived and so is the 64-entry
progress CRC table the upgrade driver reads a device's progress from. A file that cannot
produce a usable image is rejected here, where the person who wrote it can still fix it,
rather than half way through a transfer that has already erased a device. The `422` names
the offending line. The rejections that matter operationally:

- no rule lines at all - an empty rule memory has the same CRC (`f1e8ba9e`) as a device
  that has just entered programming mode, so such a job would report itself finished
  before sending anything and leave the tracker with no application
- a rule id outside 0-63, a hole in the rule ids, a duplicate id, a rule longer than 32
  data bytes, or a rule whose bytes are all zero - each one makes the transmitted rules
  and the progress table disagree, which stalls a transfer with no way to diagnose it
- two rules leaving the rule memory with the same CRC, which would make progress
  unreadable
- any compiler error line in the file

The bytes are stored verbatim, so the exact file can be downloaded again and an installed
app traced back to it. An app is immutable once uploaded: a changed application is a new
upload, which is what lets a running job trust the copy it reads on every tick.

Re-uploading a file the caller already holds does not fork the library. The same bytes
always produce the same rule memory, so a second row would only be an ambiguous duplicate
to pick from when starting an upgrade. Such a request returns `200` with the stored app and
`deduplicated: true` rather than `201`, and the stored app is returned untouched - a
different `name` or `description` on the re-upload is ignored, since an app is immutable.
The match is per uploader and on content alone: two users may each hold their own copy of
the same file.

200.description:
Success - the caller already had this file, so nothing was created and the stored
application is returned.

deduplicated.description: Present only on this response, to tell it apart from a fresh upload.

get.description:
Download the uploaded `.vso` file exactly as it was stored, so an application running on a
tracker can be matched back to a file on disk and recompiled. Served as an attachment named
after the uploaded file.

Return one uploaded application with its parsed metadata, including the `mapData` the listing
leaves out. An application the caller has no read access to is reported as missing rather
than forbidden; the `403` is the caller's role lacking device access at all, which is decided
before any app is looked up.

delete.description:
Remove an uploaded application and the stored `.vso` file behind it. Requires admin access
to the app.

An application that an unfinished upgrade still references is refused with `409`, and the
message names the jobs holding it: the upgrade driver re-reads the app on every watchdog
tick to decide which rule to send next, so deleting it would strand every device that has
already been put into programming mode. Cancel those jobs first. Jobs that have already
settled keep the app's name, hash and target CRC on themselves, so they stay readable after
the app is gone.

get.description:
Return the caller's 20 most recent app upgrade jobs, newest first. Every job carries its
devices with their rule counters, so a list can draw progress without one detail call per
job; the per-rule log is only on the detail endpoint, and is projected away here rather than
sent and discarded.

post.description:
Upgrade the VSM application on a set of LoRa trackers over the air, from an app already
uploaded with `POST /vsm-apps`.

What a device goes through: its LNS downlink queue is flushed, then an fPort 15 `df`
downlink puts it into programming mode, which empties its rule memory. From that moment the
device runs no application - it answers with the CRC of its rule memory and nothing else.
The rules are then streamed a few frames ahead of the last one the device has confirmed,
each confirmation being a CRC uplink that says how far the image has got, and a final `fc`
saves the rules and restarts the device.

Two consequences worth planning around. Queued downlinks for the target devices are
discarded by the flush, so sequence other configuration after the upgrade. And a device
whose transfer is abandoned part way stays without a working application: it keeps
reporting its rule-memory CRC on port 15 and can be upgraded again, but it will not report
telemetry until an upgrade succeeds.

Duration is set by the data rate and the duty cycle, not by Yggio. The floor for a
64-rule application at a 1% duty cycle is roughly 8 minutes at DR5, 26 minutes at DR3,
105 minutes at DR1 and over 3 hours at DR0, and those ignore uplink airtime and gateway
contention. A job running for hours on slow-reporting trackers is normal. Devices are
admitted in waves of `maxConcurrentDevices`, because a gateway cannot receive while it
transmits and programming many devices through one gateway destroys the CRC uplinks the
transfer depends on.

Returns immediately with the job ids; follow progress on
`GET /app-upgrade-jobs/{appUpgradeJobId}/detail`.

Devices whose model is known and is not a Sensative VSM LoRa tracker, and devices behind an
LNS which cannot queue and flush downlinks (only ChirpStack can), are recorded as `skipped`
and receive nothing. A device whose model Yggio does not know is still attempted. Unless
`force` is set, a device already running this application is skipped too. The caller must
have write access to every requested device and to the connector, and no device may already
have an upgrade in flight.

_id.description: The app upgrade job, used for the progress endpoints.

jobId.description: The standard job, used for generic job tracking.

delete.description:
Remove several app upgrade jobs in one request, so a long list can be cleared without one
call per job.

Only the caller's own jobs are matched, so ids belonging to another user are silently
skipped rather than reported as missing: compare `deletedCount` with the number of ids you
sent if you need to know.

Only finished upgrades may be removed. If any id names an upgrade that is still `pending` or
`running` the whole request is refused with 409 naming those ids, and nothing is deleted -
the job document is the only state the driver has, so deleting it would abandon every device
mid-programming. Cancel those upgrades first, which stops them and flushes their downlink
queues.

deletedCount.description: How many of the requested jobs were the caller's and were removed.

get.description:
Return the full app upgrade job, including per-device transfer state and the per-rule log.
This is the endpoint the progress view polls; it stops polling once the job reaches a
terminal status.

Read the two rule counters together: `lastConfirmedRule` is what the device has proven it
holds, `lastQueuedRule` is what has been handed to the LNS. Progress is only ever credited
up to what has been queued, so the pair also tells you whether frames are being lost.

Only the user who created the job can read it.

put.description:
Cancel an app upgrade. Devices still waiting for a slot are left untouched, nothing further
is sent, and the downlink queue of every device in flight is flushed so frames already
handed to the LNS are dropped instead of arriving later.

A device that was already in programming mode is left with a partial rule set and no
running application: it keeps reporting only its rule-memory CRC until an upgrade succeeds
on it. Cancelling stops sending; it does not roll a device back.

The answer comes back once the upgrade has been recorded as cancelled and its devices settled,
which is what stops every driver. The downlink queues are then flushed in the background, since
that is one LNS round trip per device and a large fleet cannot be flushed inside a request.

Only an upgrade that has not finished can be cancelled: one that completed or failed while the
page was being read is refused with 409 rather than rewritten as operator-cancelled. Only the
user who created the job can cancel it.

get.description:
Return the standard job that tracks this app upgrade, with one item per device.
For per-device rule progress use `/app-upgrade-jobs/{appUpgradeJobId}/detail`.

delete.description:
Remove a finished app upgrade job. This deletes the progress record only: downlinks already
queued on the LNS for a device the upgrade had finished with may still be delivered.

An upgrade that is still `pending` or `running` is refused with 409 - its job document is the
only state the driver has, so deleting it would leave every device draining the rule frames
already queued, dropping out of programming mode with a partial rule memory and reporting
nothing, with no record left to flush their queues or to tell a later upgrade they are busy.
Cancel it first, which stops the upgrade and flushes the devices it had programmed.

get.description:
Who owns each of several images, in one request.

The owner is the user who uploaded the image. It is not a field on the image: the access
engine records it when the image is created, and this reads it from there. Nothing copies
it onto the document on purpose, because POST /access-rights/change-owner accepts an image
and a copied field would go stale the moment ownership moved.

A grid showing twenty cards would otherwise make twenty calls, so this answers for a page
at once, the way GET /images/usage-counts does, and keys on the same ids.

Every image says whether the caller owns it. The owner's id is named only to a caller who
owns or administers the image, the same rule as GET /access-rights/resource/{id}:
a caller who can only read an image learns whether it is theirs and nothing more, so sharing
an image does not reveal who uploaded it to everyone it reaches.

An image the caller may not read is left out entirely, so absence says nothing about
whether it exists. An image with no recorded owner is answered as not the caller's rather
than failing the request, so one such image does not cost the rest of the page its answer.

Images created by Yggio itself, which is every dataListingIcon and dataListingImage, are
owned by the yggio-core user and name it to every caller who can read them, since it is no
one's identity.

One of the Images page's own routes: an account without the `image_browser_active` flag is
refused with 403 `IMAGE_BROWSER_NOT_ENABLED`.

parameters.name: imageIds
parameters.description: Between 1 and 100 image ids. Repeat the parameter for each.

get.description:
How many resources hold each of several images, in one request.

The per image route, GET /images/{id}/usage, is one call per image. A grid showing twenty
cards would make twenty, so this answers the same question for a page at once. It returns
totals only; use the per image route for the list of what holds one.

An image nothing holds comes back as 0. An image the caller may not read is left out
entirely, so absence says nothing about whether it exists.

Same limitation as the image list: an icon reachable only through the device or app that
shows it, rather than through the image itself, is left out. Such an image cannot appear in
the image list either, so it has nothing to be counted for.

It also counts the same four categories as GET /images/{id}/usage: mapOverlay, widget,
devicePhoto and floorPlan. An owned image, meaning a deviceIcon, appIcon, dataListingIcon or
dataListingImage, is pointed at by its owner rather than holding a pointer back, so it
answers 0 even while its owner is showing it. Do not gate a delete on this number: deleting
such an image is refused separately, by the check on the owner.

One of the Images page's own routes: an account without the `image_browser_active` flag is
refused with 403 `IMAGE_BROWSER_NOT_ENABLED`.

Deletes an image.

uses it, then delete it.

A deviceIcon or appIcon that its device or app still shows cannot be deleted here;
change or remove the icon on the device or app instead, which deletes the image unless a
widget or device also uses it.

200.description: The image as changed, without its bytes.

get.description:
Get the metadata of an image.

deviceIcon images are also readable by anyone who can read the device they are bound to, and
appIcon images by anyone who can read the app they are bound to, or by every user when that app is public.

What is currently using an image, for the mapOverlay, widget, devicePhoto and floorPlan
categories. Those are the four with no pointer back from the image, so a widget holding it in
settings.imageId and a device holding it in photos are what this counts.

It does not cover the owned categories. A deviceIcon, appIcon, dataListingIcon or
dataListingImage is pointed at by its owner's iconImageId or imageIds, which this does not
read, so one of those answers zero even while its owner shows it. Deleting one is still
refused: Image.deleteOne guards those four separately through assertNotShownByOwner.

total counts every resource holding the image, including ones the caller cannot read, so that
a caller cannot be told an image is free simply because the dashboard or device using it is
not shared with them. visible names only the resources the caller may read, which is the
smaller list and may be empty while total is not. A total above zero is also what refuses
DELETE /images/{id}.

A widget is named through the dashboard it sits on, since that is where access is held. A
widget on a dashboard the caller cannot read, and one on no dashboard at all, are counted in
total and left out of visible.

visible holds at most 100 entries and is a sample, not the whole set. total is exact whatever
its size, so a client showing the list can always say how many more there are. Widgets and
devices each keep half the room unless the other kind needs less, so an image held by both
never reports one kind as absent because the other filled the list. The sample is drawn from
what the caller may read rather than cut down to it, so a readable holder is listed however
many unreadable ones there are.

One of the Images page's own routes: an account without the `image_browser_active` flag is
refused with 403 `IMAGE_BROWSER_NOT_ENABLED`.

Get the image file.

deviceIcon images are also readable by anyone who can read the device they are bound to, and
appIcon images by anyone who can read the app they are bound to, or by every user when that app is public.

StatsAlignmentInQuery.name: alignment
StatsAlignmentInQuery.description:
How `distance` buckets are placed. Only used together with `distance`.
- `calendar`: buckets are calendar-aligned in `timezone`: whole seconds, minutes, hours, days or weeks, with weeks starting on Monday. A `distance` that is a multiple of a unit (for example 7200 or 172800) is counted in that unit from local midnight on 2000-01-01, so bucket edges never move with `start`. Days and weeks are counted in local calendar days and always start at local midnight. Hours, minutes and seconds are counted in elapsed time, so a multi-hour bucket (for example 10800) starts one local hour later after the clock springs forward. The first and last bucket may be partial and are returned as they are.
- Absent (deprecated): legacy alignment. Bucket times are shifted to line up with `start`, so they move whenever `start` moves, and `sum`/`count` are counted over windows that are not the returned buckets. Legacy alignment will be removed in a future major release; send `alignment=calendar`.

`valueFunction=timeWeightedMean` always uses legacy alignment.

StatsTimezoneInQuery.name: timezone
StatsTimezoneInQuery.description: IANA time zone name, for example `Europe/Stockholm`, that calendar buckets follow, including across daylight-saving changes. Only used with `alignment=calendar`. Defaults to UTC. An unknown time zone returns 400.

StatsDensifyInQuery.name: densify
StatsDensifyInQuery.description: When `true`, buckets without data between `start` and `end` are added and filled according to `fillMethod`. Only used together with `distance`. A request that would produce more buckets than the server's points limit (10000 by default) returns 400; increase `distance` or shorten the range.

StatsFillMethodInQuery.name: fillMethod
StatsFillMethodInQuery.description:
How buckets added by `densify=true` get their value.
- `linear`: interpolated between the neighbouring buckets.
- `locf`: the last bucket's value is carried forward.

deviceIds.description:
The devices to subscribe or unsubscribe. The caller must have write access to

`true` subscribes the devices, replacing any existing subscription; `false`

VsmAppCreateBody.description:
The file part plus at most the two text fields below. Any other form field is rejected with
`422`, a parsed field such as `targetCrc32` included: those are read out of the file, so a
request that sets one is claiming something the file does not say.

file.description:
The compiled `.vso` application file, as text. At most 64 kB: a full 64-rule
application with comments and a schema map is a few kB, so anything larger is not
a rule file. The extension is checked, since a `.vso` has no media type of its own.

name.description: Display name. Defaults to the uploaded file name without its extension.

deviceIds.description:
The devices to upgrade, without repeats. The caller must have write access to
every one of them, and none of them may already have an upgrade in flight.

connectorId.description: The LNS connector the devices belong to.

appId.description:
The uploaded application to program. Must be one the caller can read; it cannot be
deleted while this job is unfinished, because the driver reads it on every tick.

force.description:
Program devices that already report this application's CRC instead of recording
them as `skipped`. Reinstalling costs the device the whole transfer and leaves it
without an application while it runs, so this is off by default.

firmwareMode.description:
Which downlink behaviour the target devices tolerate.

Dots firmware before the duplicate-payload fix hangs hard when the device receives
the same fPort 15 payload twice, and a hung tracker needs physical attention. Under
`legacy` the driver therefore never queues a payload the device may already hold
within one job: it
asks a silent device for its checksum once rather than repeatedly, and it fails a
device that re-enters programming mode mid-transfer instead of re-streaming rules that
device already received. A rule the reported CRC has proven absent is still resent,
because that is the device's first receipt rather than a repeat.

`modern` is for firmware carrying the fix, where a repeat is only a wasted downlink.
The driver may then re-ask a silent device and resume one that restarted, so fewer
upgrades need a second attempt.

Yggio cannot read which release a tracker runs, and the release that carries the fix
is a firmware fact rather than a platform one: **confirm it with Sensative before
selecting `modern` for a fleet.** Selecting `modern` for a tracker without the fix can
hang it; selecting `legacy` for one that has it costs nothing but the occasional
second upgrade.

Defaults to `legacy`: a needless second job costs an operator a few minutes, while a
repeat sent to old firmware costs a site visit.

enterProgrammingTimeoutMinutes.description:
How long a device is given to pick up the programming command before it is failed.
The command only leaves the LNS on the device's next uplink, so size this on the
reporting interval of the slowest tracker in the set, not on the transfer.

maxConcurrentDevices.description:
How many devices are programmed at once. Devices sharing a gateway lose each
other's CRC uplinks, so lower this for a dense site rather than raising it.

jobIds.description: The app upgrade jobs to remove. Only the caller's own are matched.

RuleV2Definition.description: A directed acyclic graph of trigger, condition and action nodes.

entryNodeId.description: Id of the trigger node where execution starts.

RuleV2GraphNode.description: A trigger, condition or action node, discriminated by `type`.

config.description: Discriminated on resourceType. Each config is strict, so sending a field belonging to another kind - `event` on a timer, say - is rejected.

RuleV2EventTriggerConfig.description: The trigger kinds driven by a device event rather than a clock.

RuleV2DeviceGroupTriggerConfig.description: Fires like a device trigger for any device that is a member of one of the groups when it reports. Membership is read per event, so a device added to a group later is covered without editing the rule. The saving user needs read access to each group, and the rule runs for a member only if its owner can read that device.

event.description: The engine raises `updated` and `missingExpectedReport`, as for a device trigger.

RuleV2AstroTriggerConfig.description: Fires at a sun event for a fixed location, shifted by an offset.

offsetMinutes.description: Negative fires before the sun event, positive after.

RuleV2TimerTriggerConfig.description: Fires on a wall-clock schedule evaluated in `timezone`, which is what keeps a 22:00 rule at 22:00 across a daylight-saving change. Carries no `event`.

timezone.description: IANA time zone the schedule is evaluated in.

every.description: Step, restricted to values dividing the unit evenly (minutes 1-6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30; hours 1-4, 6, 8, 12).

filters.description: Devices the fire is fanned out over, one run each.

RuleV2ConditionOperand.description:
A condition operand is either a field path into the event data (`path`)
or a fixed `value`. Exactly one is set.

RuleV2ActionConfig.description:
Action configuration, discriminated by `kind`. Messaging actions
(send-email, send-sms, send-http, send-mqtt) reference a connectorId and
carry an executionPolicy; write-log writes a log entry against the rule, or
with deviceSource trigger-device against the device that triggered the run,
and carries an executionPolicy but no connectorId; trigger-rule runs another
rule without that rule's own trigger having matched; noop does nothing.

message.description: write-log only. Supports {{path}} templating from the triggering event.

deviceSource.description: send-lorawan-downlink, update-device and write-log. Where the target device comes from. device-group is send-lorawan-downlink only. write-log takes only trigger-device and is optional there: without it the log goes on the rule, as it also does for a run with no device or a device the rule owner cannot write to.

deviceGroupId.description: send-lorawan-downlink only, when deviceSource is device-group. Every current member of the group (up to 500) receives the downlink.

confirmed.description: send-lorawan-downlink only. Request a confirmed downlink.

type.description: write-log only. Severity of the written log entry.

triggerNodeId.description: trigger-rule only. Trigger node in the target rule to start from; omitted runs the whole target rule from every one of its triggers.

sourceHandle.description: Required on edges leaving a condition node; true or false branch.

triggeredBy.description: Present when this run was started by another rule's trigger-rule action.

unresolvedPath.description: Redundancy checks only. The operand path the re-read device did not carry, when that is why the check came back unsatisfied.

deviceId.description: The device a LoRaWAN downlink or device update addressed, or the device a write-log logged on. Absent for a write-log that logged on the rule.

ruleId.description: trigger-rule only. The rule this action ran.

When set, the calculation is re-run without an explicit perform call.

- `event`: re-run whenever a source device reports a new value.
- `periodic`: re-run on a schedule.

CalculationLastValueMethod.description: Aggregation applied to the last values of the sources.

CalculationWindowMethod.description: Aggregation applied over the window of the single source.

The window to calculate over. Either a number of readings (`range`) or a time span
(`time` plus `unit`).

range.description: Number of most recent readings to calculate over.

sources.description: The devices and paths whose last values are aggregated.

Calculation.description:
A calculation. `type` selects the shape:

- `lastValue`: aggregates the last value of one or more sources.
- `window`: aggregates a window of readings from a single source.

CalculationWrite.description: Payload for writing a calculation. `type` selects the shape, as for reads.

result.description: The calculated value. `null` when the sources hold no data to calculate from.

AlmanacAutoUpdateSettings.description:
A device's automatic-almanac-update subscription, stored on the device itself under
`almanacAutoUpdate`. A periodic sweep starts a real almanac push for any subscribed device
whose last push is older than `intervalDays`.

connectorId.description:
The connector each automatic push is routed through, resolved when the subscription was
created: the device's own if it had one, otherwise the one the request named.

enabledBy.description:
Whose authority each automatic push runs with. Stored rather than resolved later,
because a device's owner is not necessarily anyone who may send through its connector.

lastPushAt.description:
When an almanac was last pushed to this device, automatically or by hand. Null means
the device is due at the next sweep.

lastAttemptAt.description:
When a push was last attempted. Gates a retry backoff, so a device whose push cannot
be created is not retried on every sweep.

lastError.description:
Why the last attempt did not produce a push, or null if it did. Retryable: the sweep
tries again after its backoff. A data rate below the push's floor lands here, since
ADR can move it back above.

unsupportedReason.description:
Set when a push reached the device and could send it nothing for a reason that will not
change on its own - a network server with no downlink command the almanac can use. The
sweep stops considering the device until the subscription is written again, so a device
that moves to a supported network server needs its subscription re-saved.

AlmanacAutoUpdateRow.description: One subscribed device in the automatic-update listing.

enabled.description: What the request asked for, echoed back.

AlmanacFleetJob.description: An over-the-air GNSS almanac push and the transfer state of every device in it.

jobId.description: The standard job that mirrors this push for generic job tracking.

almanacHash.description: sha256 of the almanac image, so a push is pinned to one image.

almanacSizeBytes.description: Always 2580; the fetcher rejects any other size before sending.

watchdogLeaseUntil.description:
Internal. Every integration-api instance runs its own almanac watchdog, so a job is
leased before it is driven and exactly one instance advances it at a time. Null when
no instance holds it; a past value means the previous holder died and the job is up
for grabs again.

watchdogOwner.description: Internal. Which instance holds the lease, for diagnosing a stuck transfer.

AlmanacFleetDevice.description: One device's progress through the almanac transfer.

dr.description: Data rate, which decides the chunk size and therefore the chunk count.

confirmedChunks.description: Count of acknowledged chunks; a restart resumes from here.

retryCount.description: Consecutive failures on the current chunk, not a lifetime total.

crc.description: The checksum the device reported. 0 for the END frame, which sends none.

completedVia.description:
How the chunk was confirmed. `stall` means the device never confirmed it and the
transfer was assumed complete after the retransmit budget ran out.

VsmAppSummary.description:
An uploaded Sensative VSM application (`.vso`) and what parsing it produced, as the library
listing returns it. The rule frames, the 2048-byte rule-memory image and the progress CRC
table are derived at upload for the upgrade driver and are never part of any response, and
the application's input/output map is left out of the listing because it runs to tens of kB
per app - read one app to get it.

name.description: Display name, defaulting to the uploaded file name without its extension.

fileHash.description: sha256 of the stored bytes, lowercase hex. Two uploads of one file share it.

ruleCount.description: Number of rules in the file, 1 to 64.

ruleIds.description:
The rule ids present, always 0 to `ruleCount` - 1. Holes are rejected at upload: a rule
that needs no downlink leaves the progress CRC table ambiguous.

lastRuleId.description: The highest rule id, i.e. `ruleCount` - 1. Reaching it completes a transfer.

targetCrc32.description:
CRC32 of the fully loaded 2048-byte rule memory, unsigned. This is the value a device
reports on fPort 15 once it runs this application, so it is also how a tracker's
`vsm.rulesCrc32` identifies which app is installed. Read it in hex to compare with a
device shadow.

sensorMaskHex.description:
The sensor mask from the file's `S` line as lowercase hex without a `0x` prefix, `0`
when the file has none.

requiredSensors.description:
The sensors the mask names, decoded with the file's own `M sensor` lines. Informational:
Yggio does not refuse a device for lacking a sensor.

allOf.description: One application with the map the listing leaves out.

mapData.description:
The application's input/output map, verbatim from the file's `M output` / `M input`
lines. This is what a translator uses to name the values a device reports, so a
device running a freshly uploaded app needs it to be decoded correctly. Returned by
the single-app route and by the upload response only, never by the listing.

AppUpgradeJobSummary.description:
An over-the-air VSM application upgrade and the transfer state of every device in it, as the
listing returns it: every progress counter, but not the per-rule log.

jobId.description: The standard job that mirrors this upgrade for generic job tracking.

appName.description: Copied at start, so the job stays readable after the app is deleted.

appFileHash.description: sha256 of the app the job started against, copied at start.

targetCrc32.description: The rule-memory CRC a device reports once the upgrade has landed.

force.description:
Whether devices already reporting `targetCrc32` were programmed anyway instead of being
recorded as `skipped`.

firmwareMode.description:
Which downlink behaviour this upgrade assumed. Under `legacy` the driver never queues a
payload the device may already hold, because Dots firmware before the duplicate-payload fix
hangs on a repeat. Which release carries the fix is a firmware fact Yggio cannot read from
the device; confirm it with Sensative before starting an upgrade in `modern`.

enterProgrammingTimeoutMinutes.description:
How long a device is given to pick up the programming command. A queued downlink only
leaves the LNS on the device's next uplink, so this is sized on the reporting interval
of the slowest tracker in the job, not on the transfer itself.

maxConcurrentDevices.description:
How many devices are programmed at once. Devices beyond it stay `pending` until a slot
frees up; the cap exists because concurrent transfers through one gateway lose each
other's uplinks.

watchdogLeaseUntil.description:
Internal. Every integration-api instance runs its own upgrade watchdog, so a job is
leased before it is driven and exactly one instance advances it at a time. Null when
no instance holds it; a past value means the previous holder died and the job is up
for grabs again.

watchdogOwner.description: Internal. Which instance holds the lease, for diagnosing a stuck transfer.

allOf.description:
One upgrade with the per-rule log the listing leaves out. Returned by the detail endpoint
only: the log is up to one entry per rule for every device in the job, and nothing but the
detail view reads it.

AppUpgradeDeviceSummary.description: One device's progress through the rule transfer, without its per-rule log.

lnsType.description: The LNS integration behind the device. Only ChirpStack can be programmed.

dr.description:
Data rate at the last uplink, which decides how long the transfer takes: a 64-rule app
needs minutes at DR5 and hours at DR0.

jobItemId.description: The item of the standard job that mirrors this device.

status.description:
`skipped` devices were never touched. Everything from `entering_programming` onwards has
had its rule memory erased, so a device that ends `failed` from one of those states is
left without a running application until an upgrade succeeds on it.

skippedAsCurrent.description:
Set on a `skipped` device that already ran the requested app. Such a device is a success,
not a fault, so a job whose devices were all skipped this way completes rather than fails.

lastConfirmedRule.description:
Highest rule id the device has proven it holds, or -1 before the first confirmation.
Derived by matching the reported CRC against the app's progress table, and only ever
moved forward.

lastQueuedRule.description:
Highest rule id handed to the LNS, or -1 before the first frame. Progress is never
credited above it, so a device whose reported CRC matches a later rule is treated as an
anomaly rather than as progress.

lastReceivedCrc.description: The last rule-memory CRC read from the device, unsigned.

sameCrcCount.description:
How many times in a row the device has reported the CRC it already had. Enough repeats
mean the queued rules never arrived, and the missing ones are worked out and re-queued.

retryCount.description: How many recovery rounds this device has needed.

lnsFailureCount.description:
Failed LNS calls for this device. A device is failed once they pile up rather than
having frames thrown at an LNS that is not answering.

baselineCrc32.description:
What the device reported before anything was sent. Rule progress is only credited once
the empty rule-memory CRC has been seen, so a device that already ran this application
cannot have its old CRC mistaken for a finished transfer.

lastQueuedPayloadHex.description:
The last payload handed to the LNS for this device. Under `firmwareMode: legacy` the driver
compares against it and refuses to queue the same payload twice, because firmware without
the duplicate-payload fix hangs on a repeat.

pokeCount.description:
How many `00` checksum requests this device has been sent. Under `firmwareMode: legacy` it is
allowed exactly one, since `lastQueuedPayloadHex` only remembers the most recent payload and
a rule frame queued in between would otherwise let a second one out.

pokeAwaitingReply.description:
Whether a checksum request is outstanding. The device shadow's report timestamp moves on every
uplink on any fPort, so an unchanged CRC only counts as the device answering while this is set.

phaseEnteredAt.description: When the current status was entered, which is what its deadline is measured from.

lastProgressAt.description:
Last time a rule was confirmed. A transfer that reports but stops accepting rules is
abandoned 30 minutes after this, which bounds the gap between rules rather than the
transfer itself - a slow one legitimately runs for hours. The separate four-minute
deadline runs off the last report, not off this.

lastPokeAt.description: Last time a silent device was asked to report its rule-memory CRC.

saveQueuedAt.description:
When the save-and-restart frame was handed to the LNS. The `saving` status is entered before
the frame goes out, so this is what separates "waiting for the save to be delivered" from
"the save still has to be queued", and keeps one transient LNS error from discarding a
finished transfer.

allOf.description: One device with the per-rule log the listing leaves out.

AppUpgradeRuleLog.description: One rule of the transfer, from the first time it was queued.

attempts.description: How many times the rule was sent, so a marginal link shows up per rule.

completedVia.description:
How the rule was confirmed. `recovery` means it went missing and was re-sent after the
missing set was worked out from the reported CRC.

DashboardHeaderSettings.description: How the dashboard title and description are drawn. Every field is optional.

titleFontWeight.description: CSS font weight. The control panel offers `400`, `500` and `700`.

fontFamily.description: CSS font family, for example `Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif`.

name.description: Name shown in the dashboard list.

title.description: Heading shown at the top of the dashboard.

WidgetLayout.description:
Where a widget sits on the dashboard grid. The control panel uses a grid of 24 columns
with rows 25 px high, so `x + width` should be at most 24. The API stores any number.

x.description: Column of the left edge, from 0.

y.description: Row of the top edge, from 0. Widgets are packed upwards, so a large value puts the widget last.

DashboardWidget.description: A widget as returned inside a dashboard, with its layout, template and settings.

BrokenDashboardWidget.description:
A widget whose stored settings no longer match its template, or that is missing. It is
returned instead of failing the whole dashboard. Fix it with
`PUT /dashboards/{dashboardId}/widgets/{widgetId}` or remove it.

template.description: The stored template, or `unknown` when the widget is missing or has none.

error.description: Why the widget failed, for example `settings.field: Required` or `Widget not found`.

DashboardWithLayout.description:
A dashboard whose widgets hold only their id and layout, as returned by create, update and
duplicate. Fetch the dashboard to get the widget templates and settings.

LocationV2NodeFields.description: The fields a location and a zone share.

type.description: The kind of place in free text, trimmed, for example `building`, `floor` or `room`.

icon.description:
Icon key from the navigation widget's set: building, apartment, home, location, compass,
map, dashboard, layers, store, arrow, city, factory, warehouse, navigation, signpost,
route, target, launch, arrowOutward, light, bolt or sensors. Any key matching the pattern
is stored.

LocationV2LngLat.description: Where the location is, as a GeoJSON point.

coordinates.description: `[longitude, latitude]`: longitude from -180 to 180, latitude from -90 to 90.

LocationV2Address.description: Postal address. Every field is optional, trimmed and at most 100 characters.

LocationV2Scopes.description: The caller's access scopes, for example `read`, `write` and `admin`.

LocationV2.description: A location with the caller's access scopes on it, as returned by create, fetch and update.

Zone.description:
A zone with the caller's access scopes on it, as returned by create, fetch, update and the
dashboard routes.

locationId.description: The location the zone is in. It cannot change.

floorIndex.description: The floor the zone is on.

dashboardIds.description: The dashboards in the zone that the caller can read, in display order.

LocationV2TreeLocation.description:
A location in the tree. One the caller can read (`access: full`) has every field. One the
caller sees only because it can read something in it (`access: path`) has only `_id`,
`name`, `icon`, `type`, `lifecycle` and `lnglat`, and empty `scopes`.

zones.description:
Sorted by name. A zone the caller cannot read and that holds no dashboard it can read
is left out.

LocationV2TreeZone.description:
A zone in the tree. One the caller can read (`access: full`) has every field but
`dashboardIds`. One the caller sees only because it can read a dashboard in it
(`access: path`) has only `_id`, `locationId`, `name`, `icon`, `type`, `lifecycle` and
`floorIndex`, and empty `scopes`.

dashboards.description: The dashboards in the zone that the caller can read, in display order.

LocationV2AlarmCounts.description: Distinct devices, each counted once at its worst open alarm.

high.description: Devices with an unacknowledged `high` log and no unacknowledged `severe` one.

unmonitored.description: Devices that exist but that the caller cannot read, so their alarms are not counted.

devices.description: Devices on the node's dashboards that the caller can read.

grantableDeviceIds.description: The ids of those devices that the caller administers and so can share.

alreadyReadable.description: With a `user` subject only. How many of `grantableDeviceIds` the user can already read.

LocationV2Access.description: Who has access to a location or zone, and at which share level.

direct.description: The users and user groups the location or zone is shared with, and its owner.

inherited.description:
Zones only. The users and user groups that reach the zone through a share on its
location, at that level, and the owner.

subjectType.description:
Only `user` and `group` can be shared from these routes. `orgUnit` is an organization
unit's access group, and `unknown` an access group that no longer exists.

subjectId.description:
The user's id or the user group's id. For `orgUnit` and `unknown`, an internal
access-group reference.

displayName.description: The username, or the group's name when the caller can read the group; otherwise `null`.

level.description: The share level, always `manage` for the owner. `null` when the subject's access matches no level.

drift.description:
`true` when the subject's stored access does not match its level, for example after a
change that stopped half way. Setting the level again repairs it.

LocationV2Reason.description:
Why a call on a location or zone was refused. Refusals by the role check, the id check, the
rate limit and the request validation are plain text instead.

| `reason` | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LMV2_NOT_ENABLED` | 403 | The caller lacks the `locations_v2_active` account flag |
| `FORBIDDEN` | 403 | The caller can read the location, zone or dashboard but lacks `scope` on it; without `scope`, it does not own the location it deletes |
| `LOCATION_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The location does not exist, or the caller cannot read it |
| `ZONE_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The zone does not exist, or the caller cannot read it |
| `DASHBOARD_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The dashboard does not exist, or the caller cannot read it |
| `SUBJECT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | There is no such user or user group |
| `SUBJECT_IS_OWNER` | 409 | The owner always has full access, so it cannot be given a level |
| `DASHBOARD_IN_OTHER_ZONE` | 409 | The dashboard is in another zone |
| `ZONE_CHANGED` | 409 | A zone changed during the call; try again |
| `LOCATION_NOT_EMPTY` | 409 | The location still has zones |
| `LMV2_BUSY` | 409 | Another change held the location for over 3 seconds; try again |
| `LMV2_TOO_MANY_NODES` | 413 | Too many locations, zones or dashboards to show at once |
| `ZONE_LOCATION_IMMUTABLE` | 422 | An update tried to change a zone's location or dashboards |
| `LOCATION_FULL` | 422 | The location already has 500 zones |
| `ZONE_FULL` | 422 | The zone already holds 200 dashboards |
| `NOT_SAME_SET` | 422 | The new order is not exactly the zone's dashboards |
| `LOCATION_INVALID`, `ZONE_INVALID` | 422 | The stored location or zone is corrupt; any call that reads it can answer this |

scope.description: With `FORBIDDEN`, the scope the call needs.

zoneCount.description: With `LOCATION_NOT_EMPTY` or `LOCATION_FULL`, how many zones the location has.

capacity.description: With `ZONE_FULL`, how many dashboards a zone can hold.

limit.description: With `LMV2_TOO_MANY_NODES`, the most locations (2000) or zones (20000) that can be shown.

zoneId.description: With `DASHBOARD_IN_OTHER_ZONE`, the zone holding the dashboard, when the caller can read it.

WidgetBody.description:
A widget's template and settings. Pick the `template` first; the `settings` object that
goes with it is described in the matching schema below.

Settings point to other resources by id, so fetch those first:
- `deviceId`: an iotnode `_id` from `GET /iotnodes`. A `field` is a path into that device,
  for example `temperature` or `value.co2`. `GET /iotnodes/{id}/stats/fields` lists the
  fields that have history (needed by the chart templates).
- `imageId`: an image `_id` from `GET /images` (category `widget` for the image widget,
  `floorPlan` for floor plans, `mapOverlay` for the map widget).
- `ruleV2Id` and `triggerNodeId`: a rule from `GET /rules-v2` and the id of one of its
  trigger nodes with resource type `button`.
- `targetDashboardId`: another dashboard `_id` from `GET /dashboards`.

Settings with a default may be left out; the stored widget then has the default.
For most templates unknown settings keys are rejected with `422`; `image` and
`floorPlan` silently drop them instead.

width.description: Width in grid columns (24 columns in the control panel).

height.description: Height in grid rows (25 px each in the control panel).

WidgetCreate.description:
Body of `POST /dashboards/{dashboardId}/widgets`: the widget size plus its template and
settings. See `WidgetBody` for how settings refer to other resources.

WidgetWithLayout.description:
A widget with its layout, template and settings, as sent in `widgets` when creating a
dashboard.

Color.description: A CSS colour, either a hex value such as `#2169a8` or a colour name such as `blue`.

ThresholdOperator.description: How the value is compared with the threshold. Leaving it out means `gt`.

ValueThreshold.description: Colours the value when it matches the threshold.

value.description: The number to compare with, or `true`/`false` for boolean fields.

ChartThreshold.description: Draws a horizontal line at `value` in the given colour.

TimestampFormat.description: How a timestamp value is shown. Leaving it out shows the raw value.

DeviceItem.description: One device field shown by the widget.

field.description: Path to the value on the device, for example `temperature`.

label.description: Label shown instead of the field name.

unit.description: Unit shown after the value, for example `°C`.

ChartTimePeriod.description:
Time span the chart shows, ending now. `custom` uses `customFromTime` and `customToTime`.
Note the spelling `fiftenMinutes`.

ChartResolution.description:
Length of each data point bucket. `full` uses every stored value; `custom` uses
`customResolution`.

ChartType.description: How the series are drawn. Leaving it out draws lines.

ChartYAxisRange.description: `auto` fits the axis to the data; `fromZero` always starts it at 0.

ChartCalculation.description: How the values inside one bucket are combined.

CommandButtonsWidget.description: Buttons that run a rule (rule v2) when pressed, for example to send a command to a device.

ruleV2Id.description: The rule to run, a rule `_id` from `GET /rules-v2`.

triggerNodeId.description:
Id of a trigger node in that rule whose `config.resourceType` is `button`.
Pressing the button calls `POST /rules-v2/{ruleV2Id}/execute` with this node.

icon.description:
Icon key: power, light, play, stop, pause, lock, unlock, refresh, bolt, alarm,
thermostat, water, air or sensors. An unknown key shows no icon.

iconOnly.description: Show only the icon, without the label.

DataTableWidget.description: A table with one row per device and one column per field, with optional bar gauges and colour thresholds.

fields.description: Field paths shown for this device, for example `temperature`.

columnConfigs.description: Column settings keyed by field path.

field.description: The field path, the same as the key.

displayName.description: Column heading shown instead of the field path.

colorMode.description: Whether a threshold colour is applied to the text or the cell background.

thresholds.description: Colour thresholds. Unlike other templates they have no `operator`.

min.description: Lower bound of the bar gauge.

max.description: Upper bound of the bar gauge.

fieldOrder.description: Field paths in the order the columns are shown.

deviceColumnConfig.description: Settings for the first column, which holds the device name.

customHeading.description: Heading shown instead of the default one.

showExportButton.description: Show a button that exports the table as CSV.

DeviceChartWidget.description: A time-series chart of one field on one device.

field.description: Field with stored history, one from `GET /iotnodes/{id}/stats/fields`.

customResolution.description: Bucket length in seconds. Used when `resolution` is `custom`.

customFromTime.description: Start of the chart when `timePeriod` is `custom`.

customToTime.description: End of the chart when `timePeriod` is `custom`.

DeviceValueWidget.description: The current value of one field on one device, as text, circle, bar or gauge.

field.description: Path to the value on the device, for example `temperature`.

barDirection.description: Orientation of the `bar` display. Leaving it out means horizontal.

minValue.description: Lower bound for the circle, bar and gauge displays.

maxValue.description: Upper bound for the circle, bar and gauge displays.

shouldShowThresholdsArc.description: Draw the threshold ranges around the gauge.

booleanTrueLabel.description: Text shown when a boolean value is true.

booleanFalseLabel.description: Text shown when a boolean value is false.

showSparkline.description: Draw a small history line under the value.

EqualizerWidget.description: Live values of several device fields drawn as vertical bars.

minValue.description: Bottom of the bar scale. Leaving it out scales from the current values.

maxValue.description: Top of the bar scale. Leaving it out scales from the current values.

FloorPlanWidget.description: Device markers placed on a floor plan image, coloured by their values.

FloorPlanSettings.description: Unknown keys are dropped, not rejected.

x.description: Marker position on the image. `null` means not placed yet.

showValue.description: Overrides the widget-wide `showValue` for this device.

markerScale.description: Overrides the widget-wide `markerScale` for this device.

hiddenValueFields.description: `deviceValues` fields not shown on this device's marker. Omitted means every value is shown.

deviceValues.description: Fields that can colour the markers, each with its thresholds.

field.description: Path to the value on the device.

unit.description: Shown after a numeric value on the marker, for example `°C`.

value.description: A number, a boolean, or a string matched exactly (with `eq`).

displayText.description: Text shown instead of the value when this threshold matches.

isStarred.description: The starred value colours the marker itself when one of its thresholds matches. At most one value is starred.

markerScale.description: Marker size as a scale of the default marker, where 1 is 30 px (10 px for `dot`).

overlayField.description: Device field path (for example `contextMap.seat`) drawn on each marker. Empty means none.

numberValues.description: Put each value's letter in `deviceValues` order in front of it on the markers, the hover tooltip and the legend, such as `a) 21 °C`.

valueBackgroundColor.description: Colour of the box behind the values. Value text without a rule colour turns white on a dark colour.

showName.description: Show the floor plan name as a heading.

showControls.description: Show the zoom (+/-) buttons and the "..." menu.

showLegend.description: Show the legend of the device values' colours.

GeomapWidget.description: A tracking map showing where devices are now and the trail of their recent positions.

deviceId.description: Iotnode `_id` of a device that reports a position.

alias.description: Short label shown instead of the device name.

trailLength.description: Number of past positions kept per device. 0 shows only the current position.

tileLayer.description:
Base map style: street, satellite, humanitarian, topo, esriStreet, esriTopo or esriGray.
An unknown value falls back to street.

ImageSettings.description: Unknown keys are dropped, not rejected.

LogsWidget.description: A filtered, live list of logs (the same logs as `GET /logs`).

LogsSettings.description: Every setting is a filter or display option, so `{}` is valid and shows device logs.

resourceType.description: Show logs of this resource type.

message.description: Show only logs whose message matches this text.

acknowledgedBy.description: Username of the user who acknowledged the log.

timeFilter.description: Old relative filter as `N:unit`, for example `24:hours`. Use `timeRange`.

timeRange.description: Time window. Leaving it out shows all dates. A relative start with a `now` end keeps the list live.

alignToUnit.description: Round the start down to the start of this unit.

MapWidget.description: A map of devices, optionally limited to a saved map view and with an image overlay.

viewId.description:
A saved map view. Map views are stored by the control panel backend (`/map-views`),
not by this API.

imageId.description: Image `_id` of a `mapOverlay` image (from `GET /images`) drawn on the map.

createGeofenceEnabled.description: Let users draw geofences from the widget.

MultiDeviceChartWidget.description: A time-series chart with one series per device and field pair.

field.description: Field with stored history, one from `GET /iotnodes/{id}/stats/fields`.

customResolution.description: Bucket length in seconds. Used when `resolution` is `custom`.

hiddenLegendIndices.description: Indexes into `deviceFieldPairs` of series the user has hidden.

MultiDeviceValueWidget.description: A grid of current values from several device fields.

colorMode.description: Whether a threshold colour is applied to the tile background or the value text.

globalColor.description: Colour for every tile. Empty means each item's own colour.

globalThresholds.description: Thresholds for every tile, on top of each item's own.

NavigationWidget.description: A button that opens another dashboard.

targetDashboardId.description: The dashboard to open, a dashboard `_id` from `GET /dashboards`.

icon.description:
Icon key: building, apartment, home, location, compass, map, dashboard, layers, store,
arrow, city, factory, warehouse, navigation, signpost, route, target, launch,
arrowOutward, light, bolt or sensors.

PieChartWidget.description: One field across several devices, where each slice is one device's share of the total.

field.description: Path to the numeric value read on every device.

alias.description: Short label shown instead of the device name.

ResourceCountWidget.description: The number of resources of one kind the user can see.

SwimlaneWidget.description: One lane per device field with values scrolling past in real time.

windowSeconds.description: Visible time window in seconds. The widget loads this window's history on open.

fontStyle.description: Older style setting. `bold` and `italic` take over once set.
